opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is something a lot of people in the safety community underrate. There's a tendency to think of "what the companies care about" as almost in tension with safety, as though if a lab wants it, it must be capabilities work in disguise, and real safety research is whatever nobody else is paying attention to. I think that's often backwards.

If you want your research to actually change what happens when powerful systems get built and deployed, someone at a frontier developer has to pick it up and use it. That's much easier when the work solves a problem they already feel. If a technique makes models more reliable, makes evaluations more trustworthy, or catches some failure mode before it embarrasses them in deployment, you don't have to argue very hard for adoption. The incentives do a lot of the work for you.

That said, I'd distinguish two things. One is choosing problems where safety and commercial interest genuinely overlap: robustness, honesty, monitoring, understanding why a model did something weird. Those are great, and you get a lot of leverage. The other is problems the companies care about mostly because they're on the critical path to capabilities. There you should ask what counterfactual impact you're having, since they'll probably solve it anyway, and whether you're accelerating things you'd rather not accelerate.

The other thing I'd emphasize is timing and form. A lot of academic safety work is directionally right but arrives in a form that's hard to use: a toy setting, a method that doesn't scale, a paper with no clear story about how it plugs into a training pipeline. If you understand how these systems are actually built, you can frame your work so it's obvious how someone would adopt it. That doesn't mean giving up on long-term or speculative problems. Some of the most important work is stuff nobody is paying for yet. But even there, it helps to have a story like "when you hit this problem in two years, here's the thing you'll want," and to build relationships so that when the moment arrives, people know your work exists.

So my advice is roughly this. Spend real time understanding what practitioners are struggling with. Look for the overlap between that and what you think matters for reducing catastrophic risk. And be honest with yourself about whether you're doing something that wouldn't happen otherwise, or just doing the company's job for them under a safety label.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main thing I'd want people to understand is that there's a pretty big difference between "problems that are important for safety in the abstract" and "problems that a lab is actually going to act on." And a lot of safety researchers, especially people coming from academia or from the more theoretical side of the field, tend to optimize for the first and then get frustrated when the second doesn't follow.

The way I'd put it is: a lab is going to care about a problem to the extent that it's on the critical path to something they're already trying to do. So if you can show that a safety technique makes the model better at following instructions, or more reliable, or less likely to do something embarrassing in deployment, that gets picked up quickly, because there's already a team whose job depends on that. Whereas if you say, "here's a problem that will matter once models are much more capable than they are today," that's a much harder sell internally, even if everyone nods along and agrees it's important. There's no owner for it, there's no metric that moves, and there's always something more urgent.

I don't think that means you should only work on near-term stuff. I actually think some of the most valuable work is exactly the stuff labs aren't naturally incentivized to do. But you should be clear-eyed about which category you're in. If you're in the second category, your theory of impact probably shouldn't be "the lab will adopt this next quarter." It's more like: you're building the understanding, the tooling, the evaluations, so that when the problem does become salient, there's something ready to go, and there are people who already know how to think about it. That's a legitimate strategy, but it's a different strategy, and it requires patience.

The other thing I'd say is that "what the company cares about" isn't static, and researchers have more influence over it than they often assume. A lot of what labs care about now, things like evaluations for dangerous capabilities, or interpretability as a real research program, started as stuff a small number of people pushed on for years before it got institutional buy-in. Part of the way you make a problem something the company cares about is by making it legible: concrete evaluations, demonstrations, something you can show to a decision-maker that makes the risk feel real rather than hypothetical. Arguments alone don't do much. Demos do a lot.

So I guess the summary is: understand what's actually on the critical path, be honest with yourself about whether your problem is there or not, and if it isn't, your job is partly research and partly making the problem undeniable to the people who'd have to act on it.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing is that “a problem AI companies care about” and “a problem that matters for safety” aren’t mutually exclusive categories. You want to understand why the company cares about it, and whether solving it would actually reduce the risks you’re concerned about.

For example, a company might want to know whether its model will reliably follow instructions in situations it hasn’t seen before. That can be a product concern, but it can also be relevant to alignment. The important question is what your research establishes. Does it give us evidence about reliability in the situations where failures would be consequential, or does it just improve performance on a particular benchmark?

There’s also a practical advantage to working on problems people actually face: you get feedback. Someone can tell you, “That assumption doesn’t hold in our setup,” or, “We couldn’t use this because it’s too expensive.” Those are useful things to learn early.

But I wouldn’t make company interest your entire criterion. Some important safety problems won’t be pressing commercial concerns. I’d treat it as one useful signal, alongside your own argument for why solving the problem would make advanced AI safer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between choosing a problem that a company cares about and letting the company decide what counts as success. You want your work to be relevant to decisions people are actually going to make. But you still need an independent argument for why solving that problem would make AI safer.

One reason to talk to people at companies is that it’s very easy to have an inaccurate picture of what their bottlenecks are. You might spend six months developing a technique, imagining that someone will plug it into their training process, and then discover that it requires an assumption they can’t satisfy, or that it doesn’t give them the information they need. Finding that out early is valuable.

At the same time, ‘a company would use this’ is not sufficient. They might use it because it improves capabilities, or because it makes an evaluation easier to pass, without addressing the risk you were concerned about. So I’d ask two questions separately: Why would someone adopt this? And what changes about the risk if they do? Ideally, you have a pretty concrete answer to both.
